subject: [PATCH] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer noted that the alignment of __memcpy() itself is not relevant, but rather the alignment of the replacement in .altinstr_replacement, and requested a specific change to mitigate RET instructions in the lower half of a cache line

Reviewer David Laight pointed out that if __memcpy() is not aligned, the relocated RET in the replacement might be in the second half of a cache line and would require mitigation, but the current patch uses a mitigation-free ret.
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 3 Nov 2026 14:14:50 +0000
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

So the RET in the replacement is in the first half a cache line- so becomes a ret.
But, unless __memcpy() is aligned, the relocated RET might be in the second
half so would need mitigating - but you copy in a mitigation-free ret.

If that is the only mitigation then wouldn't aligning memcpy mean you could
just use a ret (possibly followed by an 'int 3' - or whatever is the 'flavour
of the month' instruction for stopping SLS).

David

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary:
Author corrected David Laight's understanding of how RET instructions are handled in the code, explaining that a RET in the first half of a cache line keeps the jump to its_return_thunk safe and does not require mitigation.

Author acknowledged that the REP MOVSB replacement in .altinstr_replacement needs alignment, but decided not to align __memcpy() itself due to performance considerations on certain CPUs.
reviews.raw_body:
It's the other way round: a RET in the first half keeps the jump to
its_return_thunk, see cpu_wants_rethunk_at():

        return !((unsigned long)addr & 0x20);

So the copy is the thunk jump, which is safe in either half.

---

It isn't the only one: with the retbleed, SRSO or call depth tracking
thunk every return needs it, so the code has to use RET and let
apply_returns() pick. For ITS alone, aligning __memcpy() would save one
direct jump on FSRM CPUs with ITS (Ice Lake to Rocket Lake), which I
don't think is worth it.

[...]

2026-11-03.patch_summary: This patch modifies the x86 library to use REP MOVSB instructions for large memcpy() operations on ERMS CPUs that lack FSRM support. The change addresses a potential issue where a RET instruction in the lower half of a cache line could cause problems. To mitigate this, the replacement code is modified to swap the RDX and RCX registers, which makes it easier to review and maintain.
